content:
Two caricatures meet in debates between Muslims and Christians. Muslims are told that their religion offers no assurance of forgiveness, only a scale of deeds. Christians are said to believe that they may sin freely, because Jesus (peace be upon him) has already paid the bill.[1]

Neither describes the other tradition. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches all command repentance, and Islam grounds forgiveness in the mercy of God. The disagreement lies in what makes reconciliation with God possible.

This article aims to provide context to that disagreement, insha'Allah, in six differences, each drawn from the texts the traditions themselves teach. The Quran's frame is short: "He is the One that accepts repentance from His Servants and forgives sins: and He knows all that ye do" (42:25).[2]

The Quran describes God accepting repentance again and again. "Despair not of the Mercy of Allah: for Allah forgives all sins", it says to those who have wronged themselves, and then, "Turn ye to our Lord (in repentance)" (39:53 to 54).[3]

Tawbah means turning back to God. Al-Nawawi gives its conditions as leaving the sin, regretting it and resolving never to return to it, with a fourth where another person was wronged: restoring that person's right.[4]

Christianity also teaches that God forgives, and it places that forgiveness in Christ. Paul writes, "while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). The Westminster Confession says that God justifies believers "by pardoning their sins" and "by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them".[5] Both religions say that God forgives. Christianity says He forgives through Christ, and Islam says He forgives the one who turns to Him.

Paul names what he "received" and handed on: "that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4).[6] The churches model the atonement in different ways, and they agree that the death and resurrection of Jesus are the ground of salvation.

The Quran says of Jesus: "they killed him not, nor crucified him, but so it was made to appear to them", and "Allah raised him up unto Himself" (4:157 to 158).[7] Islamic repentance therefore works with no atoning death behind it. We set out the verse in our article on the crucifixion and Quran 4:157.

"Every soul draws the meed of its acts on none but itself: no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164). The rule returns in 53:38 to 39: "man can have nothing but what he strives for".[8]

Christian theology affirms personal responsibility as well. Paul's pairing of Adam and Christ adds a bond of the whole race: mankind is affected by Adam, and saved through Christ. The churches read the bond differently. The Catholic Catechism says original sin in Adam's descendants is not a personal fault, while the Westminster Confession speaks of Adam's guilt being imputed.[9] We set out those differences in our article on original sin.

Islam teaches no salvation earned by a tally of deeds. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) told his Companions that no one's deeds would save him, and when they asked whether that held for him too, he answered that it did, unless God covered him with His mercy.[10]

Christianity teaches that salvation is a gift. Protestant theology states it as justification by grace through faith, and Catholic theology holds that even the first movement of conversion is the work of grace.[11]

The difference lies in where grace works. For the churches, grace is bound to the saving work of Christ. For Islam, the mercy of God forgives the repentant sinner directly, with no incarnate redeemer and no atoning death.

Islam has no sacrament in which a priest absolves private sin. A Muslim confesses his sin to God alone, and where he has wronged another person, his repentance may require that person's pardon or the return of what he took.[4]

The Christian traditions differ among themselves. The Catholic Catechism calls confession to a priest "an essential part of the sacrament of Penance".[12] The Orthodox Church in America describes "an open and heartfelt confession of sins", usually made today in the presence of the priest, followed by a prayer of absolution.[13]

Many Protestant churches require no confession to a priest. The Westminster Confession binds every man "to make private confession of his sins to God", and one who has wronged his brother to declare his repentance "to those that are offended".[14] The slogan "Christians confess to priests, Muslims confess to God" fits Catholic and Orthodox practice, and leaves out most of Protestant Christianity.

Islamic repentance is more than saying astaghfirullah while intending to go on. "Turn to Allah with sincere repentance", the Quran commands (66:8), and the conditions of tawbah include leaving the sin and restoring what was taken.[15]

Christianity also rejects repentance without change. The Catholic Catechism defines contrition as "sorrow of the soul and detestation for the sin committed, together with the resolution not to sin again", and tells the penitent to "repair the harm", for example to "return stolen goods".[16] The Westminster Confession says repentance is no "satisfaction for sin", and yet "of such necessity to all sinners, that none may expect pardon without it".[14]

The contrast, then, lies in the theology around repentance. On the need for it, both traditions speak with one voice.

The bottom line

Islam and Christianity share more of the vocabulary of repentance than polemic admits. Both require sorrow, a changed life, the mercy of God and the repair of harm done to others, and both deny that salvation is earned.

Their disagreement lies beneath those practices. The churches see reconciliation with God made possible by the death and resurrection of Jesus. Islam holds that the mercy of God is enough to forgive the sinner who repents, with no atoning death and no transfer of guilt, since "no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164).[8] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The first caricature is answered by the hadith in note 10, and the second by Westminster Confession of Faith 15.3 and Catechism of the Catholic Church 1451, in notes 14 and 16.
  2. Quran 42:25, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Quran 39:53 to 54, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  4. Al-Nawawī, Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn, chapter 2, "On Repentance", introduction.
  5. Romans 5:10 to 11 (World English Bible); Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), chapter 11, section 1.
  6. 1 Corinthians 15:1 to 8 (World English Bible).
  7. Quran 4:157 to 158, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  8. Quran 6:164; 53:38 to 39, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  9. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 404 to 405; Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 6, section 3.
  10. Sahih al-Bukhari 6463 and Sahih Muslim 2816 (numbering of sunnah.com), our paraphrase.
  11. Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 11, sections 1 to 2; Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1428 and 2010.
  12. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1456.
  13. Orthodox Church in America, "Penance", in The Orthodox Faith, vol. 2, Worship, "The Sacraments".
  14. Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 15, sections 3 and 6.
  15. Quran 66:8, translated by A. Yusuf Ali; al-Nawawī, Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn, chapter 2.
  16. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1451 and 1459.
